_note: Write for your reader: short lessons shown in the 7 C's guide. Ideas follow Purdue OWL's business writing pages (tone, audience, and prioritizing concerns) and plain-language guides. Every line except 'bad' must pass the app's own checks (tests/preaches.test.ts).
source: Based on Purdue OWL's business writing guides and plain-language guides.

lessons.title: Fix the big problems first
points: Start with what's missing and whether your point is clear. Then look at order and tone.
Save spelling and word choice for last. A perfect sentence in the wrong place still has to move.
The 7 C's check screens go in this order for that reason.

lessons.title: Write from the reader's side
points: Ask what the reader gets out of your message, and say that part first.
Use "you" and "your" when it's about them. Use "I" when you take the blame or make a promise.
lessons.bad: We are pleased to announce that our office will now open at 8 a.m.
lessons.good: You can now stop by our office as early as 8 a.m.

lessons.title: Giving bad news
points: Thank the reader or name a point you agree on first.
Say the no in plain words, with one reason. Don't hide it in the middle.
Offer one real next step if you have one. Don't blame a person by name.
lessons.bad: Unfortunately due to policy reasons beyond our control your request cannot be processed at this time.
lessons.good: Thank you for asking about a refund. We can't refund an order after 30 days, but we can replace the part for free. Reply to this email and we'll ship it Monday.

lessons.title: Asking politely
points: "Please" alone can still sound like an order. A question sounds kinder.
Try "Could you…", "Would you be able to…", or "I'd appreciate it if…".
Give the reason in one short sentence, and a real date.
lessons.good: Could you send me the W-2 form by Friday, Nov 13? I need it to finish my taxes.

lessons.title: Plain words aren't simple-minded
points: Use the words your reader uses. Plain writing isn't talking down to them.
Short headings and short paragraphs help a busy reader find their part.
Put the main point in the first paragraph. Put what to do next in the last.
